name: Markelle Fultz
notes: Washington's electric, do-everything freshman (23.2/5.9/5.7, best Pac-12 scoring season in two decades), a consensus No. 1 whose blend of athleticism and playmaking had no real pre-draft red flags on tape. Philadelphia took him 1st. What followed remains one of the sport's strangest medical mysteries: a shoulder condition (later diagnosed as thoracic outlet syndrome) wrecked his shooting mechanics almost immediately, limiting him to 33 games over two Philly seasons shooting 33%. A 2019 trade to Orlando and years of rehab produced only flashes (a 28-point, 15-assist game) before a torn ACL and a slide into journeyman territory — Sacramento, then G League and 10-day deals with Toronto by 2026. Bust: a consensus 1-1 talent derailed almost entirely by an unprecedented medical situation.

name: Lonzo Ball
notes: UCLA's nation-leading assist man as a freshman (14.6/7.6/6.0 on 55/41% shooting), elite vision and feel undercut by a genuinely unorthodox shooting motion that worried scouts about long-term reliability. LA Lakers took him 2nd. Ball battled injuries throughout — shoulder, knee, ankle — rebuilt his shot into a real weapon after a trade to New Orleans (37.8%, later 42% in Chicago), but a cascade of knee surgeries (meniscus and cartilage transplant) wiped out two full seasons before a brief 2024 return and a quiet exit via Cleveland and Utah by 2026. Mixed outcome: the playmaking vision and even the shooting fix were real, but injuries prevented the two-way stardom once projected.

name: Jayson Tatum
notes: A five-star Duke freshman (16.8/7.3, missed 8 games with a foot injury) LeBron James called "built for stardom" — real perimeter skill and IQ, tempered only by a thin one-and-done sample. Boston took him 3rd. Tatum delivered about as fully as a No. 3 pick can: a 5-time All-Star, multiple All-NBA First Teams, a 30.1 ppg season (a Celtics record), 2023 All-Star Game MVP, and the 2024 championship as Boston's best player. A ruptured Achilles in the 2025 playoffs interrupted the peak, but he returned in March 2026 on a record $314M extension. Hit: as complete a superstar outcome as the draft produces, injury notwithstanding.

name: Josh Jackson
notes: A five-star Kansas freshman (16.3/7.4/3.0/1.7 stl/1.1 blk, Big 12 Freshman of the Year) with all-around tools but real positional-fit questions — undersized for the four he sometimes played, unclear NBA role. Phoenix took him 4th. A promising rookie year (13.1 ppg, All-Rookie) proved to be the peak; production steadily eroded through Memphis, Detroit and Sacramento (career 11.3 ppg) before he faded out of the league within six seasons. Bust: the all-around flashes never resolved into a defined, translatable NBA role.

name: De'Aaron Fox
notes: Kentucky's blur-quick lead guard, the consensus No. 6 recruit in his class, whose explosive transition game was undercut by one clear flaw scouts flagged early: an unreliable jumper. Sacramento took him 5th. Fox developed into a franchise cornerstone anyway — a 5-year, $163M extension, a first All-Star nod and the inaugural Clutch Player of the Year in 2023, a 60-point game in 2024, and after a 2025 trade to San Antonio a second All-Star selection and a run to the 2026 Finals on a $229M extension. Hit: the exact shooting flaw scouted never fully resolved, but the athleticism and competitiveness carried him to genuine stardom anyway.

name: Jonathan Isaac
notes: A five-star Florida State forward who'd grown six inches in high school into a switchable "combo forward" (12.0/7.8/1.5 blk, All-ACC Freshman), lottery-grade defensive versatility. Orlando took him 6th. Isaac developed into a legitimate two-way starter by his third season (11.9/2.3 blk), but an August 2020 bubble ACL tear wiped out an entire season, and further hamstring and adductor injuries turned the rest of his career into a series of short, injury-interrupted stints (52-71 games a year at reduced production) — briefly waived and immediately re-signed by Orlando in 2026. Mixed outcome: real two-way starter-level talent that a brutal injury chain never let fully play out.

name: Lauri Markkanen
notes: A Finnish Arizona freshman dubbed "the best shooting 7-footer college basketball has ever seen," elite size-shooting combination with an obvious NBA translation. Minnesota took him 7th (traded to Chicago). Markkanen set an NBA record with ten threes in his first three games and had a solid four-year Chicago run, but it was a trade to Utah that unlocked full stardom — 2023 Most Improved Player and first All-Star selection (25.6 ppg), a $238M extension, and a franchise-record 51-point game in 2025-26 at a career-high 26.7 ppg. Hit: the shooting-size unicorn projected at Arizona became a genuine All-Star, just on a Utah timeline rather than a Chicago one.

name: Frank Ntilikina
notes: A French pass-first point guard (Mark Cuban himself called him a "project") with real defensive versatility but clear shooting and offensive-production questions for the NBA level. New York took him 8th. Those questions proved decisive — an inefficient rookie year (36.4% FG) set the tone for an underwhelming Knicks tenure, and stops in Dallas and Charlotte never changed the trajectory. Bust at the NBA level, but Ntilikina has thrived back in Europe since — championships with Partizan (2025) and Olympiacos (2026 EuroLeague title), now at Paris Basketball — a skill set that fit Europe far better than the NBA's spacing demands.

name: Dennis Smith Jr.
notes: A five-star NC State point guard (18.1/6.2/1.9 stl, ACC Rookie of the Year, two ACC-record triple-doubles as a freshman) with explosive playmaking, tempered by a prior high-school ACL tear as the durability flag. Dallas took him 9th. Smith's rookie season (a triple-double at 20, one of the youngest ever) suggested stardom, but a trade to New York began a steady decline through Detroit, Portland, Charlotte and Brooklyn, his role shrinking every stop until he was playing G League ball with Sioux Falls by 2025. Bust: electric athletic tools that never turned into a sustained NBA role.

name: Zach Collins
notes: A four-star Gonzaga freshman center (10.0/5.9/1.7 blk in limited minutes, a 14-point/13-rebound/6-block Final Four semifinal outing) with real shot-blocking upside but a thin offensive role to evaluate. Sacramento took him 10th (traded to Portland). Collins's Portland tenure was defined almost entirely by injury — shoulder labrum surgery, multiple foot stress-fracture surgeries — limiting him to 154 games across four seasons, before a move to San Antonio finally let him show real per-game production (11.6 ppg in 2022-23). A torn labrum and, later, a wrist fracture and season-ending toe surgery in Chicago kept the injury pattern going, though he signed a two-year extension in 2026. Mixed outcome: real starting-caliber flashes whenever healthy, a career defined by durability rather than talent.

name: Malik Monk
notes: A five-star Kentucky freshman scorer (19.8/45%FG/39.7%3PT, SEC Player and Freshman of the Year), an elite shot-maker with the clearest translatable NBA skill in the class. Charlotte took him 11th. Monk's early Hornets years were inconsistent (including a 2020 substance-abuse suspension), but he found his footing as a bench sparkplug in LA and then fully broke out with Sacramento — a $78M extension and a 2024-25 season averaging 17.2 ppg, including a 45-point double-overtime outburst. Mixed outcome: the elite scoring skill scouted was always real, but it took nearly a decade and a role change to become a consistently productive NBA player.

name: Luke Kennard
notes: A Duke sophomore sharpshooter (19.5/5.1/2.5 on 43.8% from three, 85.6% FT), Ohio's second all-time high school scorer behind LeBron, a pure shot-making translation to the next level. Detroit took him 12th. Kennard became exactly that reliable movement shooter across a long, well-traveled career — Detroit, a $64M Clippers extension, Memphis, Atlanta, a brief Lakers stint with a career triple-double, and a 2026 move to Phoenix. Solid outcome: a genuine, sustained NBA shooting specialist for nearly a decade.

name: Donovan Mitchell
notes: A Louisville sophomore breakout (15.6/4.9/2.7 on 46/35% shooting) who arrived a modest 27-43 ranked recruit, athleticism and scoring instincts the appeal more than a long track record. Denver took him 13th (traded to Utah). Mitchell exploded immediately — a 41-point rookie-record game, a 2018 Dunk Contest win — and became a 7x All-Star, multiple-time All-NBA player, and after a 2022 trade to Cleveland led the Cavaliers to their first Conference Finals since LeBron's exit, signing a $273M extension. Hit: a mid-first-round bet on athleticism that became a genuine perennial All-Star.

name: Bam Adebayo
notes: A five-star Kentucky freshman (13.0/8.0, SEC All-Freshman), valued foremost for rebounding and interior physicality rather than a finished offensive game. Miami took him 14th. Adebayo developed into a true two-way anchor — first All-Star and Finals run in 2020, a $163M extension, five All-Defensive Second Teams and a first All-Defensive First Team in 2024, multiple Conference Finals and a 2023 Finals trip, and a historic 83-point game in March 2026, the second-most in NBA history. Hit: a rebounding-and-defense prospect who became a genuine All-NBA-caliber two-way star.

name: Justin Jackson
notes: UNC's ACC Player of the Year and consensus All-American as a junior, a 6'8" scoring forward whose defensive limitations were already a quiet concern beneath the college accolades. Portland took him 15th (traded to Sacramento). Those defensive concerns proved decisive at the NBA level — Bleacher Report later named him the league's worst defensive small forward — and Jackson settled into journeyman territory across eight teams (career 6.0 ppg on 42.3% FG), a 2021 championship ring with Milwaukee coming via one regular-season game rather than a real role. Bust: college-award-winning production that never solved the defensive gap scouts quietly noted.

name: Justin Patton
notes: A five-star Creighton freshman center (12.9/6.2, Big East Freshman of the Year) with real rim-running athleticism and passing feel (Vlade Divac comps), but scouts flagged rebounding positioning and foul-prone rim contests as real defensive question marks. Chicago took him 16th (traded to Minnesota). A broken foot in his first Summer League set an unfortunate tone — Patton played just 22 total NBA games (3.9 ppg) across five teams before his NBA opportunities ran out entirely. Bust: a lottery talent that injuries and the flagged defensive gaps never let develop.

name: D.J. Wilson
notes: A Michigan big man who overcame prior injury (including knock-kneed valgus deformity issues) to have a strong junior Big Ten tournament stretch (15.3 ppg) and elite shot-blocking (57 blocks, most in nine Michigan seasons), but durability and consistency were open questions given the injury history. Milwaukee took him 17th on a $12.1M rookie contract. Those durability concerns proved right — 148 total NBA games across four teams (Milwaukee, Houston, Toronto, Philadelphia) at 4.4/3.1 before his career shifted overseas by 2024. Bust: real defensive tools undercut by exactly the durability/consistency questions flagged pre-draft.

name: T.J. Leaf
notes: A five-star UCLA freshman who led the Bruins in scoring alongside Lonzo Ball (16.3 ppg on an elite 61.7% FG, First-Team All-Pac-12), a stretch-four profile that depended entirely on an outside shot that hadn't been tested much in college. Indiana took him 18th. That shot never arrived at the NBA level — just 26.5% from three over his final two Pacers seasons — and Leaf settled at 3.3/2.0 across stops with Indiana, Oklahoma City and Portland before his career shifted to China and, by 2025, Maccabi Tel Aviv. Bust: elite college efficiency inside the arc that never extended outside it as an NBA stretch four needed.

name: John Collins
notes: A Wake Forest sophomore breakout (19.2/9.8, first ACC player since Tim Duncan to hit 600/300 in a season), elite efficiency and rebounding for a big who declared early. Atlanta took him 19th. Collins developed into a legitimate scoring-rebounding forward, earning a five-year, $125M extension in 2021, before a 2023 trade to Utah, a 2025 move to the Clippers, and a 2026 sign-and-trade to Detroit. Solid outcome: a real, sustained double-double-caliber NBA forward for the better part of a decade, never quite an All-Star.

name: Harry Giles
notes: ESPN's No. 1 overall high school recruit entering Duke, but two prior ACL tears (one in each knee) and a pre-season knee surgery limited him to a token freshman season (3.9/3.8 in 26 games) — real generational talent that no one could actually evaluate healthy. Portland took him 20th (traded to Sacramento) purely on remembered upside. The injury pattern never broke: a redshirt rookie year, then journeyman stints with Sacramento, Portland, the Clippers, Brooklyn and the Lakers (career 5.4 ppg across 165 games) never let the talent show up consistently. Bust: a generational recruit whose knees, not his talent, wrote the outcome.

name: Terrance Ferguson
notes: A top-15 high schooler who skipped college to play professionally in Australia, an unconventional path built around perimeter shooting (a record 7 threes in a Nike Hoop Summit MVP outing) but with real gaps in evaluators' ability to judge his defense and IQ against complex systems. Oklahoma City took him 21st. Ferguson's lone full-starter season (6.9 ppg in 2018-19) proved to be the ceiling, with production declining every year after until he was waived by Philadelphia (career 4.5 ppg across 204 games). Bust: the shooting translated only in flashes, and the untested developmental gaps never closed.

name: Jarrett Allen
notes: A five-star Texas freshman center (13.4/8.4, including a 22-point/19-rebound outing against Kansas) on a rough Texas team, valued for fundamentals and rebounding more than a finished offensive game. Brooklyn took him 22nd, one of the youngest players ever to debut for the franchise. Allen developed into a full-time starter by his second season, and a 2021 trade to Cleveland (part of the James Harden deal) unlocked a $100M extension, a 2022 All-Star selection, and continued career-high production (a 40-point game in 2026) as a franchise cornerstone. Hit: a steady developmental big who became a genuine All-Star-caliber starting center.

name: OG Anunoby
notes: An Indiana defensive prospect already being called "the NBA's next great lockdown defender" for his size-length-athleticism combination — but a season-ending knee surgery in January 2017 cut his sophomore year short and clouded the pre-draft medical picture. Toronto took him 23rd anyway. Anunoby became exactly the elite two-way wing projected: a 2019 champion (injured for the Finals itself), a league steals leader and All-Defensive honoree, and after a 2023 trade to New York a $212.5M extension and a starring role (21.2 ppg) on the Knicks' 2026 championship team, their first title in 53 years. Hit: the lockdown-defender-plus-real-offense outcome scouts hoped for, injury risk notwithstanding.

name: Tyler Lydon
notes: A skilled, improving Syracuse forward (10.1/6.3/1.8 blk as a freshman to 13.2/8.6/1.4 blk as a sophomore, 40%+ from three both years), size and shooting touch the appeal, but a bench role at Syracuse left real readiness questions. Utah took him 24th (traded to Denver in the Donovan Mitchell deal). Lydon barely played in the NBA — one game as a rookie, 25 games the following year (0.9 ppg) — before Sacramento released him in 2019. Bust: real shooting touch that a limited college role and questionable NBA translation never let become a real career.

name: Anžejs Pasečņiks
notes: A Latvian big man (2013 FIBA U18 All-Tournament, All-Star Game MVP) taken on projection with limited detailed scouting record. Orlando took him 25th and immediately traded him to Philadelphia. Pasečņiks got only one real NBA look — 27 games with Washington in 2019-20 (5.8/4.0) — before a single-game cameo and a 2021 waiver, his career shifting to Spain, France, Turkey and Taiwan. Bust: a projection-only pick that got almost no real NBA opportunity to prove out.

name: Caleb Swanigan
notes: Purdue's unanimous All-American sophomore, an elite rebounder whose evaluators were explicit about the risk: an unrefined jumper and help defense, and a build that played more like an undersized center than a true power forward. Portland took him 26th. Those exact flaws never got fixed — 75 total NBA games across three seasons (2.4/2.9) with heavy G League time before he was out of the league by 2020. Bust: the specific weaknesses scouts flagged were exactly what kept him off NBA rosters. Swanigan died in June 2022 at age 25, of natural causes.

name: Kyle Kuzma
notes: A raw, feel-first Utah junior (16.4/9.3, First-Team All-Pac-12) still physically filling out, real shooting touch but unfinished as an overall player. Brooklyn took him 27th and dealt him to the Lakers on draft night. Kuzma made the All-Rookie First Team, won the 2020 championship as a rotation piece, then broke out fully after a trade to Washington (a career-high 22.2 ppg in 2023-24) before a 2025 trade to Milwaukee. Solid outcome: real, sustained NBA scoring production and a championship ring, never quite an All-Star.

name: Tony Bradley
notes: A five-star North Carolina recruit who backed up Kennedy Meeks as a freshman (7.5/5.1 in 14.6 minutes) on the 2017 national championship team, real offensive-rebounding instincts but a thin, reserve-role sample to judge NBA readiness. LA Lakers took him 28th (traded to Utah). Bradley settled into a real, if marginal, nine-season journeyman run across eight teams (4.3/3.8), capped by a surprising 2025 Finals trip with Indiana and a 2026 stint in Atlanta. Mixed outcome: a legitimately long NBA career as deep reserve depth, never more.

name: Derrick White
notes: An unconventional prospect — a Division II transfer to Colorado who used part of his rookie contract to pay off student loans — whose late growth spurt and First-Team All-Pac-12 breakout (18.1 ppg) as a late bloomer left real questions about whether the skill translation was legitimate against higher competition. San Antonio took him 29th. White developed gradually into a genuine two-way star: a $73M Spurs extension, then a 2022 trade to Boston where he became a starter, an All-Defensive Second Teamer, a 2024 NBA champion hitting big playoff shots, and a 2026 All-Defensive First Team honoree and Sportsmanship Award winner. Hit: one of the great late-bloomer value outcomes in recent draft history.

name: Josh Hart
notes: Villanova's senior All-American and winning glue guy, a hustle-and-defense wing whose freshman-year shooting (31% from three) improved dramatically by his final seasons — energy and IQ the carrying traits more than pure scoring. Utah took him 30th, the last pick of the first round (traded to the Lakers). Hart became one of the round's best value outcomes: a long, winning career through the Lakers, New Orleans and Portland, then a franchise cornerstone in New York — a triple-double record season (nine in 2024-25) and, alongside Jalen Brunson and Mikal Bridges, a 2026 NBA championship, the Knicks' first title in 53 years. Hit: a glue-guy college star who became a genuine winning NBA rotation fixture and champion.

name: Frank Jackson
notes: A five-star Duke recruit (No. 10 nationally) who only started half his freshman games (10.9 ppg, 40% from three) behind a loaded Duke roster, real shooting talent but a thin sample to judge. Charlotte took him 31st (traded to New Orleans). Foot surgery delayed his debut, but Jackson carved out a real journeyman NBA run (Pelicans, then Detroit peaking at 10.6 ppg) before his career shifted to the G League, Utah briefly, and China by 2022. Mixed outcome: real NBA rotation minutes for several years, never more than a bench scorer.

name: Davon Reed
notes: A four-year Miami wing (14.9/4.8) sold as a good shooter who could defend four positions — a legitimate 3-and-D case, but the kind of profile that projects as a role player rather than a sure thing, hence a second-round grade. Phoenix took him 32nd. A rookie-year meniscus surgery set the tone, and Reed never secured consistent NBA minutes (122 games, 3.1 ppg) across Phoenix, Denver and the Clippers before his career shifted to the G League, Taiwan and Latvia. Bust: real shooting touch that a lack of opportunity and injury never let become an NBA role.

name: Wes Iwundu
notes: Kansas State's career games-started record holder, a four-year, third-team All-Big 12 wing (13.0/6.3/3.5 as a senior) valued for steadiness over star upside. Orlando took him 33rd. Iwundu carved out a real three-plus-season Magic rotation role (4.8/2.5/1.0 across 182 games) before bouncing through Dallas, New Orleans and Atlanta, his career eventually shifting to the G League and leagues in Germany, Greece, Australia and Spain. Mixed outcome: a real, multi-year NBA rotation piece, never more than replacement-level.

name: Frank Mason III
notes: Kansas's unanimous, consensus National Player of the Year as a senior (20.5/5.1 on 49/47% shooting), elite efficiency and scoring undercut by a clear NBA concern: a 5'11" frame in a draft class stacked with bigger guards. Sacramento took him 34th. Mason's rookie chance (6.5/2.5 across 90 games) never grew into more, and he was waived in 2019 — a G League MVP season with Milwaukee's affiliate never converting into a real NBA recall, his career shifting to France, Lebanon, China and Puerto Rico. Bust: the exact size concern flagged pre-draft, in a class that included Mitchell and Adebayo, is what capped him.

name: Ivan Rabb
notes: A top-10 recruit and two-time All-Pac-12 big at Cal, real rebounding and shot-blocking instincts but an unrefined, inconsistent offensive game that made him more project than finished product. Orlando took him 35th (traded to Memphis). Rabb never developed past marginal reserve minutes (85 games, 5.7/4.3 across two seasons) before Memphis released him and the Knicks waived him without a single game — his NBA career over by his fourth pro season despite the elite recruiting pedigree. Bust: the offensive polish questions flagged pre-draft never resolved.

name: Jonah Bolden
notes: A four-star UCLA recruit (27 blocks in 31 games off the bench) whose athleticism and defensive versatility were real, but whose offensive game stayed minimal and whose college role was limited by a 2015 knee surgery. Philadelphia took him 36th. Bolden got a real look (51 games across two seasons, 4.3/3.4) but never secured consistent NBA minutes, and after brief stops with Phoenix he was waived in 2020 and retired from basketball entirely at 25 to pursue cryptocurrency. Bust: elite defensive tools that an unfixed offensive game — and an early retirement — never let become a real NBA career.

name: Semi Ojeleye
notes: SMU's AAC Player of the Year as a senior (18.9/6.8), a physical, switchable two-way forward whose translatable NBA skill was defense against bigger, stronger wings. Boston took him 37th. Ojeleye carved out a real four-season Celtics role as a defensive stopper (including a start that held Giannis Antetokounmpo to 16 points) before stints with Milwaukee and the Clippers, then a strong late-career shift to Europe (Virtus Bologna, Valencia, Crvena zvezda). Bust relative to a first-round-adjacent grade, though a genuinely useful NBA defensive role player for years.

name: Jordan Bell
notes: Oregon's Pac-12 Defensive Player of the Year and a Final Four run, an elite shot-blocker (a school-record 94 blocks) whose limited offensive game made him purely a defense-and-energy second-round bet. Chicago took him 38th (traded to Golden State). Bell's timing was outstanding — a champion as a rookie (2018 sweep of Cleveland) and a second Finals trip in 2019 — but his role shrank after leaving the Warriors, bouncing through Minnesota, Memphis, Washington and Chicago plus extensive G League and international stops (China, Puerto Rico). Mixed outcome: two real championship-contending seasons at the right time, but no lasting NBA role once he left Golden State.

name: Jawun Evans
notes: Oklahoma State's Big 12 Freshman of the Year who broke out as a sophomore (19.2/6.4, First-Team All-Big 12), an instinctive lead guard whose NBA translation depended on athleticism and playmaking holding up against faster, longer defenders. Philadelphia took him 39th (traded to the Clippers). Those doubts proved right — 56 total NBA games across three teams (4.4/0.9 in his best stretch) before his career shifted to the G League and Canada, Greece, Lithuania, Poland and France. Bust: elite college production that never survived the jump in competition level.

name: Dwayne Bacon
notes: A former McDonald's All-American and top-15 recruit who put up real production at Florida State (17.2 ppg as a sophomore, Second-Team All-ACC), a physical scoring wing with lottery-level pedigree despite a two-year college stay. New Orleans took him 40th (traded to Charlotte). Bacon's NBA role stayed limited throughout — a career-best 10.9 ppg with Orlando in 2020-21 was the high point of a modest 6.3 ppg career across 207 games — before he found more success internationally after being cut loose by New York and the Lakers. Bust: former blue-chip pedigree that never turned into a real NBA role.

name: Tyler Dorsey
notes: A former Parade All-American who helped Oregon to the 2017 Final Four (clutch shot-making in the run), a two-year college scorer (14.1 ppg, 45.5/41.6% shooting) seen as a developmental combo guard rather than a sure NBA contributor — hence a second-round grade. Atlanta took him 41st. Dorsey never found a real role (107 games across Atlanta, Memphis and Dallas, 6.6 ppg) before his career shifted to Europe, Israel and Turkey. Bust: real March production that never became NBA-level consistency.

name: Thomas Bryant
notes: Indiana sophomore big with a standout physical profile — 6'11" with a 7'6" wingspan and 9'4.5" standing reach, both 99th-percentile marks at the combine — plus genuinely efficient scoring touch around the rim and in the mid-range (Varejao/Jefferson comps floated pre-draft). The concern that kept him out of the first round was mobility: evaluators questioned whether he could hold up defending the pick-and-roll at NBA speed. He fell to 42nd (Lakers, via a Jazz draft-night trade). The career has played out almost exactly along those lines — a real breakout with Washington in 2018-19 (10.5/6.3 on 61% FG) validated the touch and efficiency, but the flagged mobility limitations kept him from ever locking down a full-time starting job. Nine seasons and six teams later (Lakers, Wizards, Nuggets, Heat, Pacers, now Cleveland), he's a reliable third-string/spot-minutes center (2025-26: 6.2/3.4 on 50.6% FG in 12.2 min for the Cavaliers). Solid outcome: a long, legitimately useful NBA career and one standout season, but a depth piece rather than a starter, exactly per the pre-draft scouting.

name: Isaiah Hartenstein
notes: A German-developed big man who'd already won a Lithuanian League title and King Mindaugas Cup with Žalgiris Kaunas, real rebounding and passing production (14.7/9.5 at the U18 Euros) but enough rawness to fall to the second round. Houston took him 43rd. Hartenstein needed years of G League seasoning (a 2019 G League title and Finals MVP) before establishing himself, bouncing through Denver, Cleveland, the Clippers and New York before signing a $87M deal with Oklahoma City in 2024 — where he won the 2025 championship (7/9 in the Game 7 clincher) and re-signed for $75M in 2026. Hit: a classic slow-burn international developmental big who became a championship-caliber starting center.

name: Damyean Dotson
notes: Houston's senior AAC First-Teamer (17.4/6.9 on 47/44.3% shooting), an efficient combo guard whose translatable NBA skill was shooting. New York took him 44th. Dotson needed G League seasoning before a real rookie foothold, then had a genuinely productive Knicks stretch (10.7 ppg across 73 games in 2018-19, a 30-point outburst), followed by a shorter Cleveland run and 10-day deals before his career shifted to Turkey and China. Mixed outcome: a real multi-year rotation role at his best, never sustained beyond that.

name: Dillon Brooks
notes: Oregon's 2017 Pac-12 Player of the Year (16.7/5.4/3.1 as a sophomore, consensus Second-Team All-American), a physical, defense-first scoring wing whose stock was clouded by a 2016 foot injury. Houston took him 45th (traded to Memphis). Brooks became one of the round's best value outcomes — a long-time Grizzlies starter and All-Defensive Second Teamer (2023), a $86M Rockets deal, and a full breakout with Phoenix in 2025-26 (a career-high 20.2 ppg) earning a $73M extension. Hit: a defensive-minded college star who developed into a genuine high-usage NBA scorer.

name: Sterling Brown
notes: SMU's senior wing under Larry Brown (13.4/6.5, Second-Team AAC), an efficient shooter (60.2% FG, 53.6% 3PT as a junior) whose modest athleticism capped his upside to a second-round, role-player grade. Milwaukee took him 46th. Brown carved out real rotation minutes across the Bucks, Rockets and Mavericks (a career-high 27-point game), before a brief Lakers stint and a move to Europe — Alba Berlin, Partizan Belgrade and Žalgiris Kaunas by 2026. Mixed outcome: a real several-year NBA rotation role, never more.

name: Ike Anigbogu
notes: A top-50 UCLA recruit (alongside Lonzo Ball and T.J. Leaf) who barely played as a freshman (13 minutes, 4.7 ppg) behind Thomas Welsh, valued purely for elite athleticism and defensive flashes — real offensive rawness the clear concern. Indiana took him 47th, knowing he'd need pre-draft knee surgery. That durability risk defined the career: just 14 total NBA games (0.9 ppg) across two seasons, repeated G League injuries, and a waiver by 2019 before a long gap until a 2025 signing with Vanoli Cremona in Italy. Bust: athletic upside that injuries never let get tested.

name: Sindarius Thornwell
notes: South Carolina's SEC Player of the Year as a senior (21.4/7.2/2.2 stl), an all-around, high-feel two-way guard with real production but modest measured athleticism for the wing spots he'd guard in the NBA. Milwaukee took him 48th (traded to the Clippers). Thornwell's rookie year (73 games, 3.9 ppg) proved to be the ceiling — steadily shrinking roles with the Clippers, then brief looks with New Orleans and Orlando (career 2.5 ppg across 160 games). Bust: an SEC Player of the Year whose game never scaled to NBA speed.

name: Vlatko Čančar
notes: A Slovenian forward drafted more on projection than a detailed pre-draft scouting record. Denver took him 49th and waited two years to sign him. Čančar carved out a real, gradually expanding Nuggets role (up to 60 games played by 2022-23, 3.4/1.8 career), and was on the roster (29 seconds of Finals floor time) when Denver won the 2023 championship. After brief stints with Olimpia Milano, he returned to Spain's San Pablo Burgos in 2026. Mixed outcome: a real, if marginal, NBA role and an actual championship ring, never more than deep bench depth.

name: Mathias Lessort
notes: A French big man (Élan Chalon, then Nanterre) who'd already turned down US college offers from Gonzaga and NC State to stay in Europe, winning the FIBA Europe Cup and French Cup in 2017. Philadelphia took him 50th as a pure draft-and-stash pick, his rights traded four more times over the following years. Lessort never signed with an NBA team, instead becoming a genuine European star — a EuroCup champion with Monaco, an ABA League champion with Partizan, a two-time All-EuroLeague First Teamer, and a 2024 EuroLeague and Greek League champion with Panathinaikos. Never played in the NBA — one of the class's most successful "stash" outcomes, just entirely in Europe.

name: Monte Morris
notes: Iowa State's premier point guard, setting an NCAA record for assist-to-turnover ratio (5.21) as a senior — elite decision-making and shooting, with modest athleticism and defense as the honest concerns for a lead guard. Denver took him 51st. Morris needed a two-way/G League runway before becoming a genuine, efficient backup point guard, reaching 12.6 ppg by 2021-22, then a real starting role in Washington (10.3/5.3) before a nomadic finish through Detroit, Minnesota, Phoenix, Indiana and, by 2026, Olympiacos in Greece. Solid outcome: a real, long NBA rotation career built on exactly the decision-making skill scouted, never more than a backup-caliber ceiling.

name: Edmond Sumner
notes: A three-year Xavier lead guard (14.9/4.9/4.4 as a junior) whose stock was clouded by a season-ending injury in January 2017 and a history of chronic knee tendinitis that had already cost him most of his freshman year. New Orleans took him 52nd (traded to Indiana). Sumner needed a two-way runway before earning real Pacers minutes (7.5 ppg by 2020-21), but a torn Achilles in 2021 and a brief, waived Brooklyn stint ended the NBA run — his career shifting to Lithuania and China, where he won the 2025 CBA scoring title at 36 ppg. Mixed outcome: real NBA rotation minutes eventually earned, derailed by exactly the durability concerns flagged pre-draft, with a genuine second life overseas.

name: Kadeem Allen
notes: Arizona's senior defensive stalwart (All-Pac-12 Defensive Team, 1.6 steals) whose modest scoring (9.8 ppg) raised real questions about NBA offensive viability. Boston took him 53rd on one of the league's first two-way contracts. Allen's defense never came with enough offense to hold a roster spot — 47 total NBA games (5.5 ppg, a 9.9 ppg best season) with Boston and New York before his career wound down. Bust: elite college defense that offensive limitations, flagged pre-draft, kept from becoming a real NBA role.

name: Alec Peters
notes: Valparaiso's most decorated scorer ever (school records for points and rebounds, led all of Division I in the points/rebounds top-20 double as a senior at 23.0/10.1), but a pre-draft foot stress fracture limited his workout showcase. Phoenix took him 54th. Peters got only 20 NBA games (4.1 ppg) before the opportunity dried up entirely — his career instead flourishing in Europe, where he's won multiple EuroLeague-level titles. Bust at the NBA level, a genuine European star elsewhere.

name: Nigel Williams-Goss
notes: Gonzaga's WCC Player of the Year and consensus All-American as a junior (16.8/4.7/1.7 stl on 48.6% shooting), a smart, team-oriented facilitator whose translatable NBA athleticism was the open question. Utah took him 55th. That question was answered quickly and unfavorably — just 10 NBA games (1.4 ppg) in 2019-20 before being waived — though Williams-Goss became a genuine EuroLeague winner afterward, capturing a title with Real Madrid in 2023. Bust at the NBA level, a real European champion instead.

name: Jabari Bird
notes: A former five-star, McDonald's All-American recruit who developed into a solid four-year Cal scorer (14.3/4.7 as a senior, 44/36.5% shooting), athletic wing size the appeal. Boston took him 56th. Bird's NBA chance was brief (13 games, 3.0 ppg) and effectively ended by domestic violence charges filed in September 2018 that kept him off the Celtics' roster the following season; he was traded to Atlanta and immediately waived in 2019. Bust: a once-touted recruit whose NBA career was cut short by off-court legal issues as much as performance.

name: Sasha Vezenkov
notes: A Bulgarian stretch four (Aris, Greek League MVP/Most Improved/Best Young Player in 2015) who'd committed to Xavier before choosing to stay in Greece, real size-shooting combination but minimal direct NBA scouting record. Brooklyn took him 57th, his rights traded twice more (Cleveland via the Harden deal, then Sacramento) before he finally signed a $20M deal in 2023 — a modest NBA cameo (42 games, 5.4 ppg) before a trade to Toronto and a buyout sent him back to Olympiacos, where he won the 2026 EuroLeague title and was named EuroLeague MVP. Bust at the NBA level, an outright European superstar.

name: Ognjen Jaramaz
notes: A Serbian guard (Mega Vizura) taken 58th by New York as a draft-and-stash pick after a Summer League look. Jaramaz never signed an NBA contract, instead building a steady, multi-country European career — Spain's Liga ACB, EuroLeague stints with Bayern Munich and Partizan Belgrade, and a 2026 move to Lithuania's Lietkabelis. Never played in the NBA — a legitimate journeyman European guard whose path never crossed into the league that drafted him.

name: Jaron Blossomgame
notes: Clemson's ACC Most Improved Player turned steady senior scorer (17.7/6.3, third-team All-ACC), a two-time combine invitee whose production suggested real draft interest. San Antonio took him 59th (path to Cleveland). Blossomgame's NBA chance amounted to 27 games with Cleveland (4.2 ppg) in 2018-19, more productive in the G League than the NBA, before his career shifted to Israel, Germany and France by 2021. Bust: solid, sustained college production that only got a token NBA look.

name: Alpha Kaba
notes: A French big man (Élan Béarnais, then Mega Basket in Serbia) who'd starred for French youth national teams, taken 60th — the last pick of the draft — by Atlanta as a pure projection pick. Kaba never signed an NBA contract despite his rights being traded three more times over the following decade, instead building a genuinely accomplished European career — an ABA League rebounding title, a French championship, Turkish League MVP honors, and multiple EuroCup rebounding titles across France, Serbia, Turkey, China, Spain, Israel and Korea. Never played in the NBA — the very last pick of 2017 became a real, decorated international pro.
